notes.text: He abruptly tells them; I am Joseph — They knew him only by his Egyptian name, Zaphnath-paaneah, his Hebrew name being lost and forgot in Egypt; but now he teaches them to call him by that, I am Joseph: nay, that they might not suspect it was another of the same name, he explains himself. I am Joseph your brother. This would both humble them yet more for their sin in selling him, and encourage them to hope for kind treatment. This word, at first, startled Joseph's brethren, they started back through fear, or at least stood still astonished: but Joseph called kindly and familiarly to them. Come near, I pray you. Thus, when Christ manifests himself to his people he encourages them to draw near to him with a true heart. Perhaps being about to speak of their selling of him, he would not speak aloud, lest the Egyptians should overhear, and it should make the Hebrews to be yet more an abomination to them; therefore he would have them come near, that he might whisper with them, which, now the tide of his passion was a little over, he was able to do, whereas, at first, he could not but cry out.

He endeavours to sweep their grief for the injuries they had done him, by shewing them, that, whatever they designed, God meant it for good, and had brought much good out of it. See note at "ver. 1" for start of item, ie. No. 1

Be not grieved or angry with yourselves — Sinners must grieve, and be angry with themselves for their sins; yea, though God, by his power, bring good out of them, for that is no thanks to the sinner: but true penitents should be greatly affected with it, when they see God bringing good out of evil. Though we must not with this consideration extenuate our own sins, and so take off the edge of our repentance; yet it may do well thus to extenuate the sins of others, and so take off the edge of our angry resentments. Thus Joseph doth here. His brethren needed not to fear that he would revenge upon them an injury which God's providence had made to turn so much to his advantage, and that of his family. Now he tells them how long the famine was likely to last, five years yet, ver. 6, and what a capacity he was in of being kind to his relations, which is the greatest satisfaction that wealth and power can give to a good man.

See what a favourable colour he puts upon the injury they had done him, God sent me before you — God's Israel is the particular care of God's providence. Joseph reckoned that his advancement was not so much designed to save a whole kingdom of Egyptians, as to preserve a small family of Israelites; for the Lord's portion is his people: whatever goes with others, they shall be secured. How admirable are the projects of Providence! How remote its tendencies! What wheels are there within wheels; and yet all directed by the eyes in the wheels, and the Spirit of the living Creature! See note at "ver. 1" for start of item, ie. No. [1.] [5.] He promises to take care of his father and all his family, during the rest of the years of famine. (1.) He desires that his father might speedily be made glad with the tidings of his life and honour. His brethren must hasten to Canaan, and acquaint Jacob that his son Joseph was Lord of all Egypt - He knew it would be a refreshing oil to his hoary head, and a sovereign cordial to his spirits. He desires them to give themselves, and take with them to their father, all possible satisfaction of the truth of these surprising tidings.

glossa.text: « God sent me, » etc. ((AUG. Quaest. in Gen., tom. III.)) What is it that according to other copies is read thus: « For God sent me before you, that your remnant should remain upon the earth, and that he might nourish up a great seed of your remnant? » For this does not agree in every point, etc., *as far as* « and so all Israel should be saved. »

« Thou shalt dwell in the land of Gessen, » etc. ((HIERON.)) In the Hebrew there stands *Gosen* ( )Migne prints a Hebrew word within these parentheses; our digitized source has lost it and left them empty.. Whence the error grew up that the land of Gessen is in Arabia. Further, as it stands in our codices, it is written with a final *m*, Gessem, which by no means pleases me, as signifying a land rained upon. For Gessem is turned into *rain* , where also in very many copies Gessem is found.

notes.text: Fret not — Because they prosper in their wicked enterprizes.
Commit — All thy cares and business, and necessities, commend to God by fervent prayer.
Judgment — It shall be as visible to men, as the light of the sun, at noon-day.
Rest — Do not repine at his dealings, but quietly submit to his will, and wait for his help.
Fret not — Either against the sinner for his success; or against God. Do evil - If grief arise in thee, take care that it do not transport thee to sin.
The earth — This for the most part was literally fulfilled in that state of the church.
Not be — He shall be dead and gone. Diligently - Industriously seeking him. His place - His place and estate, and glory.

But — Those who patiently bear God's afflicting hand, and meekly pass by injuries. Peace - Partly of outward peace and prosperity, which God in his due time will give them: but principally of inward peace, in the sense of God's favour and the assurance of endless happiness.

glossa.text: *A psalm of David.* This psalm is as it were the garment of Christ, which covers his whole body with precepts, and protects it from adversities, and cherishes it as in the bosom of counsel. It is a draught against those who murmur at the flowering of the wicked and the toil of the good, as though all things were done by chance, so that, spurning God, they cleave to the world. The Church therefore admonishes that no one imitate the malignant, but that whatever good is hoped for be sought from the Lord, who gives things profitable and eternal.

*The herbs of the grasses.* ((AUG.)) It is now winter, etc., *as far as* because it hath not yet appeared what we shall be.

((AUG., CASS.)) Herbs not of gardens, but of grasses, that is, the meanest, which spring up of themselves through the fields. *Hay,* the noble, who prosper easily; herbs, the middling: but both those quickly wither and these fall away.

*Cease.* ((AUG.)) Anger is sudden, fury lasting; but both are to be forsaken, through which men sin. ((CASS.)) This is said to him who is still weak, etc., *as far as* by doing it he flourishes for a time.
*And yet a little while,* etc. ((AUG.)) After this short life, etc., *as far as* nor did he feel the worm of a gnawing conscience.
*But the salvation of the just is from the Lord.* All these things are for the just, yet the whole is from God, and he gathers it up summarily.

notes.text: But some one possibly will say, How are the dead raised up, after their whole frame is dissolved? And with what kind of bodies do they come again, after these are mouldered into dust?

To the inquiry concerning the manner of rising, and the quality of the bodies that rise, the Apostle answers first by a similitude, ver. 36-42, and then plainly and directly, ver. 42, 43. That which thou sowest, is not quickened into new life and verdure, except it die — Undergo a dissolution of its parts, a change analogous to death. Thus St. Paul inverts the objection; as if he had said, Death is so far from hindering life, that it necessarily goes before it.
Thou sowest not the body that shall be — Produced from the seed committed to the ground, but a bare, naked grain, widely different from that which will afterward rise out of the earth.

But God — Not thou, O man, not the grain itself, giveth it a body as it hath pleased him, from the time he distinguished the various Species of beings; and to each of the seeds, not only of the fruits, but animals also, (to which the Apostle rises in the following verse,) its own body; not only peculiar to that species, but proper to that individual, and arising out of the substance of that very grain.

So also is the resurrection of the dead — So great is the difference between the body which fell, and that which rises. It is sown - A beautiful word; committed, as seed, to the ground. In corruption - Just ready to putrefy, and, by various degrees of corruption and decay, to return to the dust from whence it came. It is raised in incorruption - Utterly incapable of either dissolution or decay.

It is sown in dishonour — Shocking to those who loved it best, human nature in disgrace! It is raised in glory - Clothed with robes of light, fit for those whom the King of heaven delights to honour. It is sown in weakness - Deprived even of that feeble strength which it once enjoyed. It is raised in power - Endued with vigour, strength, and activity, such as we cannot now conceive.

It is sown in this world a merely animal body — Maintained by food, sleep, and air, like the bodies of brutes: but it is raised of a more refined contexture, needing none of these animal refreshments, and endued with qualities of a spiritual nature, like the angels of God.

The first Adam was made a living soul — God gave him such life as other animals enjoy: but the last Adam, Christ, is a quickening spirit - As he hath life in himself, so he quickeneth whom he will; giving a more refined life to their very bodies at the resurrection. Gen. ii, 7

The first man was from the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven-The first man, being from the earth, is subject to corruption and dissolution, like the earth from which he came. The second man — St. Paul could not so well say, "Is from heaven, heavenly:" because, though man owes it to the earth that he is earthy, yet the Lord does not owe his glory to heaven. He himself made the heavens, and by descending from thence showed himself to us as the Lord. Christ was not the second man in order of time; but in this respect, that as Adam was a public person, who acted in the stead of all mankind, so was Christ. As Adam was the first general representative of men, Christ was the second and the last. And what they severally did, terminated not in themselves, but affected all whom they represented.
They that are earthy — Who continue without any higher principle. They that are heavenly - Who receive a divine principle from heaven.
The image of the heavenly — Holiness and glory.

But first we must be entirely changed; for such flesh and blood as we are clothed with now, cannot enter into that kingdom which is wholly spiritual: neither doth this corruptible body inherit that incorruptible kingdom.

glossa.text: *But some man will say.* Hitherto he has proved the resurrection of the dead by reasons, now he shows by the very nature of things that it can come to pass; as if he should say, by these things it is proved: but nevertheless someone depraved might speak thus, as though the resurrection of the dead could not come to pass by nature: *And if they shall rise: or with what body,* as if he should say: It will not be able to be other than it now is, that is, passible and mortal. The Apostle answers: *Foolish man,* that is, thou who dost not attend to what thou daily seest in the grain.
*Foolish man, thou: that which thou sowest.* So the dead man will be able to live, and in a better body: as that which thou sowest rises better.

*But God gives.* As therefore the bare grain is sown, and by the nod of God rises again in some manner clothed, having many increases with it, so the dead man by the power of God will be able to live, and to rise again in a better body. *To every one of the seeds.* So also for us he will refashion our ancient bodies, as Job says: *Whom I myself shall see, and not another.* But there will be a difference in glory and in dignity, although they be of the same nature. As not all flesh is of the same dignity, though of the same elements, and this is what he says:
*It is sown.* That is, although a man, from the time he is conceived until his dissolution, is in corruption, and afterwards swarms with worms, yet he will rise in incorruption.

*A natural body.* That is, one which has nothing from the soul except that it is made to feel through it, as the beasts have. *It shall rise spiritual.* Passing over into the nature of spirit, that is, having certain spiritual properties, because it is nimble, light, and in no need of food. When he said that the body would pass over to incorruption, he makes mention of corruption, that the greater dignity of the resurrection may be shown. *If there is a body.* Truly a spiritual body will rise, because *if* it now is, *it is natural,* that is, it is established to be so; and at some time *it will be spiritual.* For as we are natural because our carnal father was made into a living soul: so we shall be spiritual in the resurrection: because our spiritual Father was made, in his resurrection, into a quickening spirit.

*Man.* Those two men, the first and the second, are in a manner the whole human race: born of the one, born again of the other. Christ is called Adam, because he is of the same matter; the last, because after him no other man succeeds who might be the head or the author of the human body.

*But not.* He has said that our bodies will be spiritual; but lest any should doubt whether the natural can become spiritual, he proves it by the likeness of Christ; as if he should say, he was made into a quickening spirit. *But not first* was there in him that *which is spiritual, but that which is natural, then the spiritual.* So also can it come to pass concerning us.

*The first man.* He is truly the first unto a living soul; because he was formed from the dust of the earth, natural and passible by nature. *The second man,* because *from heaven,* that is, because the divine nature was united to the human, therefore *heavenly,* that is, spiritual in the resurrection; and because the first father was earthly, such are all men. *Heavenly.* Christ is said to be so, because he was conceived and born not after the manner of men, but by the divine nod.

*And this I say.* The Jews believed in a resurrection to come, but after the manner of this life, that they should marry and beget: whence certain men could not answer the Sadducees concerning the woman of the seven husbands, for these men were thinking carnally about the resurrection: but the Apostle removes this, saying:

*That flesh.* By flesh and blood he signifies the belly and lust, that is, the works of the flesh (which will not be there).

*Neither shall corruption possess incorruption.* Lest thou shouldst think that this is said according to the substance of the flesh, he has made it plain. Therefore he said that flesh shall not possess the kingdom of God: because the corruption of mortality, which is here shown by the name of flesh, shall not possess incorruptibility.

notes.text: But I say to you that hear — Hitherto our Lord had spoken only to particular sorts of persons: now he begins speaking to all in general. Matt. v, 44.

To him that smiteth thee on the cheek — Taketh away thy cloak - These seem to be proverbial expressions, to signify an invasion of the tenderest points of honour and property. Offer the other - Forbid not thy coat - That is, rather yield to his repeating the affront or injury, than gratify resentment in righting your self; in any method not becoming Christian love. Matt. v, 39.
Give to every one — Friend or enemy, what thou canst spare, and he really wants: and of him that taketh away thy goods - By borrowing, if he be insolvent, ask them not again. Matt. v, 42.
Matt. vii, 12.

It is greatly observable, our Lord has so little regard for one of the highest instances of natural virtue, namely, the returning love for love, that he does not account it even to deserve thanks. For even sinners, saith he, do the same: men who do not regard God at all. Therefore he may do this, who has not taken one step in Christianity.
Matt. vii, 1.

Into your bosom — Alluding to the mantles the Jews wore, into which a large quantity of corn might be received. With the same measure that ye mete with, it shall be measured to you again - Amazing goodness! So we are permitted even to carve for ourselves! We ourselves are, as it were, to tell God how much mercy he shall show us! And can we be content with less than the very largest measure? Give then to man, what thou designest to receive of God.

glossa.text: *Love your enemies.* When it has been said what they can suffer from enemies, he adds how they ought to bear themselves toward those enemies. And here the Church is not fed with milk, but strengthened with the stronger food of charity. It is not enough not to hate, but what is beyond human nature is commanded, to love. And whereas the law commands a return of vengeance, the Gospel bestows charity for enmities, kindness for hatreds, prayers for curses, patience for persecutors, and even the grace of recompense for those who hunger.

*Pray for them that calumniate you.* That the prophets seem to imprecate, these are not the wishes of men desiring it, but foretellings of things to come: for they themselves prayed for their enemies.

*And to him that striketh thee.* Since charity is patient, it ought to sustain the patient bearing of him that beats; and since it is kind, it ought not to answer curses. If it *seeketh not her own,* it ought not to resist him that plunders; if it *envieth not ((I Cor. XIII))*, it ought not to hate an enemy. *Offer them,* etc. The physician of souls commands those whom he instructs to heal their neighbours to bear all things that can avail for the salvation of their neighbours. And it pertains to mercy that, as from sick and frenzied sons, they should suffer many things, if their health require it, until the infirmity pass. What is so wonderful as to offer the cheek to him that strikes? Nay, every assault of the angry man is broken, wrath is calmed; and through patience he is invited to repentance. *A garment.* What is said of the garment and the coat is to be done also in other things which by any right we call temporally our own. For if this is commanded concerning necessary things, much more is it enjoined to despise superfluous things.

*Ask not again.* Because *charity is patient, is kind ((I Cor. III))*; it not only bears bravely the injuries of an enemy, but also kindly anticipates the favour of a friend, that they may be drawn by other kindnesses.

*And as you would.* Lest he should seem to dissolve the law, he keeps in benefits the return which he neglects in injuries. Nor does he say, as they do, but *as you would that men should do to you, that you also should do to them,* that the return may be the fuller, since the act is matched with the wish. And now extend the works of charity not only to friends, but even to enemies, that they may begin to be friends; and first extend the affection of love, and afterwards the works of charity.

*And if you love.* The more eminent your degree of profession, the more needful it is that the care of virtue be more abundant, that you embrace in the bosom of charity even those who do not love.

There are two kinds of benefit: either when we give kindly what we give, or when we lend to one who will repay.

*But yet,* etc. After he has reproved as unfruitful the love and mutual benefit of sinners, he now shows how these are to be done fruitfully by the faithful, as if he should say: Although such love and mutual benefit profit not sinners, yet do you love, not only by the leading of nature, as they love friends, but by a higher degree of virtue, your enemies. The philosophers divide justice into three parts: one toward God, which is called piety; another toward parents, or the rest of the human race; the third toward the dead, that the due rites of burial be paid to them. But the Lord, having gone beyond the oracle of the law and the summit of prophecy, extended the office of piety even to those who have done hurt.

*Hoping for nothing thereby: and it shall be.* Not fixing the hope of a reward in man. For whether he repay what you have lent, God will nevertheless repay also, at whose bidding you did it; or whether he repay not, your inheritance shall be for ever.

*Be ye therefore merciful,* etc. He rains upon the evil, the earth does not deny its produce, the same sun enlightens the good and the evil.

Mystically: he waters the people of the Jews with prophetic rains, and upon those not deserving it the ray of the eternal sun has shone. If therefore they have believed, be merciful to them, by teaching and by lifting them up, and do not rashly judge, lest anyone conscious of his own offence be compelled to pass sentence upon another.

*Judge not.* There are certain middle and uncertain things, in what mind they are done, because they can be done well and ill. We know not either what he will be like who now appears evil, of whose correction to despair, and to reprove him as though cast off, is rash.

Concerning open things which cannot be done with a good mind, it is permitted us to judge.

*For with the same measure.* It can be taken generally of all things which are done by mind, by hand, by tongue, because God will render according to the works of each.

 *For with the same, ((AMBR.))* God will not repay with an unjust measure, but it is as if he should say: The very rashness of judging and the unjust measure hurts thee, punishes thee, and often not him about whom thou doest this. Or if thou judgest and measurest rightly, it profits thee, it saves thee, even though sometimes not him upon whom thou bestowest these things.

hymns.title: In the bulb there is a flower
Faith, while trees are still in blossom
Now the green blade riseth, from the buried grain
Walk in the light of God's counsel
Like a tree that's planted by the water

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: 'The first man, Adam, became a living soul' (v.45) quotes Gen 2:7 LXX ('the man became a living soul') verbatim, adding 'first' and 'Adam' to set up the antithesis with the 'last Adam' as life-giving spirit. Volume is maximal with citation formula 'it is written'; this is the chapter's anchoring OT text for the two-Adam anthropology.

echoes.text: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
echoes.note: 'The first man is of the earth, made of dust' (v.47) re-reads Gen 2:7, where God forms the man 'of the dust of the ground.' The dust/earth motif distinguishes the earthly Adam from 'the Lord from heaven'; recurrence within vv.45-49 confirms deliberate exegetical use beyond the v.45 citation.

echoes.text: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: 'Those who are made of dust' bearing 'the image of the man of dust' (vv.48-49) recalls 'dust you are, and to dust you shall return,' the mortality stamped on Adam's line. It reinforces the Gen 2:7 dust language with the death-sentence of Eden, giving the contrast its weight of perishability.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.” God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.
echoes.note: 'As we have borne the image of those made of dust, let us also bear the image of the heavenly' (v.49) invokes the creation of humanity 'in the image of God,' now patterned after the heavenly Man. The image (eikon) language is distinctively Gen 1:26-27 (cf. 5:3); coherence with Paul's Adam Christology supports a medium allusion.

echoes.text: Those who are wise shall shine as the brightness of the expanse; and those who turn many to righteousness as the stars forever and ever.
echoes.note: The graded 'glory' of sun, moon, and differing stars applied to the resurrection body (vv.40-42) echoes 'those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who turn many to righteousness like the stars.' Daniel's astral imagery of the risen righteous gives the star-glory analogy its resurrection coherence; verbal overlap on stars/glory grounds the allusion.

echoes.text: God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth”; and it was so. The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.
echoes.note: 'To each seed a body of its own' and the distinct kinds of flesh (vv.38-39) faintly echo the creation account where plants bear seed 'each according to its kind' and creatures are made by kinds. The echo is conceptual, supporting Paul's argument that God assigns distinct bodies; volume is low, hence a faint echo.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: “‘You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of your people; but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Love your enemies' radicalizes and inverts the Holiness Code's 'love your neighbor as yourself,' which forbids vengeance and grudge-bearing. The love-command and its anti-retaliation logic are directly in view; high Coherence with vv.32-36.

echoes.text: “If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall surely bring it back to him again. If you see the donkey of him who hates you fallen down under his burden, don’t leave him, you shall surely help him with it.
echoes.note: The Torah already commands aiding an enemy's straying ox or fallen donkey — concrete enemy-love. This statute is the OT seedbed of 'do good to those who hate you,' giving strong Availability and Volume for the command.

echoes.text: If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink: for you will heap coals of fire on his head, and Yahweh will reward you.
echoes.note: 'If your enemy is hungry, give him bread... ' is the wisdom tradition's enacted enemy-love, closely matching 'do good to those who hate you' and 'give to everyone who asks.' High Coherence with Leviticus 19 and Exodus 23.

echoes.text: And what you yourself hate, do to no man. Don’t drink wine to drunkenness, and don’t let drunkenness go with you on your way.
echoes.note: 'What you hate, do to no one' is the deuterocanonical negative Golden Rule, the nearest Second-Temple antecedent to 'as you would like people to do to you, do so to them.' Direct conceptual dependence; Availability within the OT/deuterocanon is secure.

echoes.text: Don’t say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will render to the man according to his work.”
echoes.note: 'Do not say, I will do to him as he has done to me' is the proverbial renunciation of retaliation behind 'offer also the other cheek' and not demanding goods back. Moderate Volume; reinforces the anti-lex-talionis thrust.

echoes.text: Let him give his cheek to him who strikes him; let him be filled full with reproach.
echoes.note: 'Let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him; let him be filled with reproach' is a striking verbal parallel to 'to him who strikes you on the cheek, offer also the other.' Notable Volume despite being a lament rather than a command.

echoes.text: I gave my back to the strikers, and my cheeks to those who plucked off the hair; I didn’t hide my face from shame and spitting.
echoes.note: The Servant 'gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pluck the beard' models nonretaliatory submission to assault, coherent with the cheek-turning saying. Figural link to the Suffering Servant pattern.

echoes.text: He that shows mercy will lend to his neighbor; And he that strengthens him with his hand keeps the commandments. Lend to your neighbor in time of his need; And pay you your neighbor again in due season.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's teaching on lending to a neighbor and showing mercy stands behind 'lend, expecting nothing back.' Faint wisdom-tradition echo of generous lending without calculation.

echoes.text: “Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel, and tell them, ‘You shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy.
echoes.note: 'Be merciful, even as your Father is merciful' is a deliberate reworking of the Holiness Code's imitatio Dei formula 'be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy.' The imitation-of-God structure is unmistakable; Luke substitutes mercy for holiness. High Volume.

echoes.text: Yahweh passed by before him, and proclaimed, “Yahweh! Yahweh, a merciful and gracious God, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness and truth,
echoes.note: The defining self-revelation 'the LORD, a God merciful and gracious' supplies the content of the Father's mercy that disciples are to imitate, and 'kind toward the unthankful and evil' echoes God's compassion on the undeserving. Strong Coherence with the imitatio Dei.

echoes.text: Yahweh is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness. He will not always accuse; neither will he stay angry forever. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities. For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his loving kindness toward those who fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us. Like a father has compassion on his […]
echoes.note: 'The LORD is merciful and gracious... as a father has compassion on his children' joins divine mercy with fatherhood exactly as Luke does ('your Father is merciful'). Moderate Volume reinforcing Exodus 34.

echoes.text: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]
echoes.note: The command to lend generously to the poor 'and your heart shall not be grieved' grounds open-handed lending without expectation of return. Coherent with Luke's generosity ethic; moderate Availability.

echoes.text: All day long he deals graciously, and lends. His seed is blessed.
echoes.note: 'All day long he deals graciously and lends' commends the righteous lender who gives freely, undergirding 'lend, expecting nothing back.' Faint wisdom-Psalter echo, low confidence.

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD, and he will repay' captures the give-and-it-will-be-given reciprocity of v.38. Coherent with the surrounding generosity teaching; moderate Volume.

echoes.text: your own iniquities, and the iniquities of your fathers together”, says Yahweh, “who have burned incense on the mountains, and blasphemed me on the hills; therefore will I first measure their work into their bosom.”
echoes.note: 'I will measure their former work into their bosom' supplies the measure-into-the-lap imagery behind 'good measure... running over, will be given into your bosom.' Faint but specific verbal contact with the lap/bosom measuring motif.

echoes.text: “‘You shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in measures of length, of weight, or of quantity. You shall have just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin. I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
echoes.note: The Torah's demand for honest measures ('a just ephah') stands behind the just-recompense logic of 'with the measure you measure it will be measured back.' Conceptual echo of measure-for-measure justice.

echoes.text: With the merciful you will show yourself merciful. With the perfect man you will show yourself perfect. With the pure you will show yourself pure. With the crooked you will show yourself shrewd.
echoes.note: 'With the merciful you show yourself merciful... with the pure you show yourself pure' is the OT measure-for-measure principle of divine requital matching human conduct, behind 'with the measure you measure.' Low and contested.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Do not fret because of the wicked; trust in the Lord and do good.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
You meant it for harm; God meant it for good.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
Love your enemies, and do good, expecting nothing in return.
Come, let us worship. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Picture a brother who was sold, given up for dead, standing now with power over the ones who wronged him.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
And instead of revenge, he weeps and forgives: you meant evil, but God turned it to life.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
This is the hard, holy way: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, give without keeping score.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
Forgive, and you will be forgiven; the measure you give is the measure you will get back.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The wronged brother weeps and forgives.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
You meant evil; God turned it to life.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful.
Love your enemies; give without keeping score.
Be merciful, as your Father is merciful. Amen.
